universal_lens: Temporal regularity and dynamic stability in gait are quantified via SampEn and LyE, capturing stride-to-stride variability and local divergence rates in kinematic trajectories. Gait retraining induces dynamic stability shifts via joint-angle variability modulation and movement regularity optimization.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian inference models gait transitions using SampEn and LyE as probabilistic observables, enabling predictive state estimation under retraining protocols. Bayesian inference models joint-angle CVs as stochastic processes; conformal prediction bounds uncertainty in movement regularity across states.

State transitions driven by biomechanical variability: HRFS-GR → HNRFS via reduced joint-angle CVs; HRFS-AN as baseline control.

primitives.name: Sample Entropy Regularity Measure
primitives.verbatim_quote: Coefficient of variation (CV), sample entropy (SampEn), and largest Lyapunov exponent (LyE) were used to characterize discrete kinematic variability, temporal regularity, and local dynamic stability, respectively.

primitives.assumptions: Time series data is stationary and sufficiently long for reliable entropy estimation; SampEn is computed with fixed parameters m=2 and r=0.25×SD.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When data points are insufficient or signal noise exceeds tolerance, SampEn becomes unreliable.

layer2.mapping: SampEn serves as a kernel for measuring temporal regularity in gait variability, enabling GSI to model movement predictability.

primitives.name: Local Dynamic Stability Index
primitives.verbatim_quote: Analyses included 13 habitual rearfoot strikers assessed during acute NRFS adoption and after 12 weeks of gait retraining, together with 14 HNRFS.

primitives.assumptions: Trajectories in phase space are reconstructed from time series; exponential divergence is measurable and stable over short timescales.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When trajectories do not diverge or converge, LyE approaches zero or negative infinity, indicating loss of chaotic behavior.

layer2.mapping: LyE quantifies instability in gait dynamics, enabling GSE to detect critical transitions in movement control.
layer2.telemetry: Rate of divergence in kinematic trajectories, used to assess local stability.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter window 3 (pages 9–12) presents a comparative analysis of movement regularity and local dynamic stability during acute and 12-week retrained non-rearfoot strike (NRFS) running versus habitual NRFS (HNRFS). The use of nonlinear dynamics provides a deeper understanding of how gait retraining affects system stability, beyond traditional linear kinematic measures. This supports a dual-process model where immediate adaptation is robust, but sustained change requires targeted interventions. The implications extend to injury prevention and performance optimization through personalized gait retraining protocols. The study compares habitual NRFS (HNRFS), acute NRFS after training (HRFS-AN), and gradual retraining (HRFS-GR). SampEn quantifies regularity by measuring the likelihood that similar patterns remain similar over time. Using m = 2 and r = 0.1 on joint angles (page 14), m = 3 and r = 0.1 on joint angles and COM (page 15), and m = 3 and r = 0.25 on joint angles and COM (page 16), the authors isolate sensitivity to embedding dimensions and tolerance thresholds. These parameters reflect the system's complexity and noise resilience. The results suggest that retraining reduces movement irregularity, especially in the sagittal plane, indicating improved local dynamic stability. This supports the hypothesis that gait retraining enhances motor control precision. The use of multiple planes (sagittal, coronal, transverse) allows for multi-dimensional analysis of gait adaptability. The statistical significance (p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001) underscores robustness of findings. The methodological framework aligns with Bayesian inference principles where SampEn acts as a probabilistic descriptor of movement regularity, enabling predictive models in GSI. In GSE, these primitives inform real-time feedback systems for athletes, mapping entropy changes to biomechanical state transitions during retraining.
